name: 52nd Street
label: Factory Records
lede: A Manchester jazz-funk band got a New Order production, a Jellybean remix and a New York club hit out of Factory, then walked out on the label and took an R&B single to No. 8 in America.

eras.title: Spotted at the Band on the Wall
eras.text: 52nd Street came together in Manchester at the end of 1980 as a jazz-funk band, and RCA and Warner Bros. both took a look. It was Rob Gretton, New Order's manager and a Factory partner, who signed them after a night at the Band on the Wall.

years.src: Wikipedia: 52nd Street (band) · Rare and Obscure Music
years.h: Tony Henry and Derrick Johnson start 52nd Street in Manchester
years.p: Henry on guitar, Johnson on bass, Desmond Isaacs on keys, Tony Thompson on drums, Jennifer McCloud singing. Singer Rose Williams and saxophonist Eric Godden come and go inside six months.
years.xp: John Dennison soon takes over the keyboards from Isaacs and Beverley McDonald replaces McCloud at the mic, the lineup that made the Factory records.

years.src: Rare and Obscure Music · Discogs: 52nd Street
years.h: A first session at Revolution Studios with Richard Searling
years.p: The Northern Soul DJ Richard Searling and Derek Brandwood oversee the band's first recordings. RCA and Warner Bros. both show interest, Discogs notes.

years.src: Rare and Obscure Music · Wikipedia: 52nd Street (band)
years.h: Rob Gretton sees them at the Band on the Wall and brings them to Factory
years.p: Gretton and [[Tony Wilson|124a6f5d-b2e0-4a75-95ad-db4c38063e02]] sign 52nd Street, a jazz-funk band on a label better known for [[Joy Division|9a58fda3-f4ed-4080-a3a5-f457aac9fcdd]] and [[A Certain Ratio|73577e86-4da8-4d76-949d-34c757e053be]].

years.src: Look I've Heard · Cerysmatic Factory: 52nd Street
years.h: Look Into My Eyes, FAC 59, is NME single of the week
years.p: [[Donald Johnson|49569ee1-aba3-4c08-8ead-9791a7f8c96d]], drummer in [[A Certain Ratio|73577e86-4da8-4d76-949d-34c757e053be]], produces. Paul Morley makes it his single of the week in NME; it still doesn't sell.

eras.title: Drum machines and Danceteria
eras.text: The band heard New York hip-hop and Bill Laswell's records and went electronic. With Bernard Sumner at the desk and Factory's New York office on the phone, 52nd Street had a dance-chart hit in America before most of Britain had heard them.

years.src: Look I've Heard · Rare and Obscure Music · Cerysmatic Factory: 52nd Street
years.h: Bernard Sumner, as "Bemusic", produces "Cool as Ice"
years.p: A demo cassette goes to Gretton early in 1983. Sumner and Donald Johnson ("DoJo") produce; Factory Benelux issues it as FBN 20.
years.xp: The band had spent late 1982 swapping their live funk for drum machines. Factory had no UK release lined up, so John Peel and Janice Long played it on Radio 1 from white labels.

years.src: Look I've Heard · Discogs: Cool As Ice · Wikipedia: 52nd Street (band)
yt: Cool As Ice, 12-inch restructured by Jellybean Benitez
years.h: Michael Shamberg gets them on A&M in six weeks
years.p: Factory's New York man lands an American deal. Jellybean Benitez restructures the 12-inch, it reaches No. 29 on Billboard's dance chart, and the band play clubs including Danceteria.
years.xp: The A&M 12-inch (SP-12058) says it is licensed from Factory Benelux via Of Factory New York, which is why a Belgian catalogue number turns up on an American record. Both sides run about seven and a half minutes.

years.src: Look I've Heard · Rare and Obscure Music · Cerysmatic Factory: 52nd Street
years.h: New Order's Stephen Morris produces "Can't Afford"
years.p: Factory has it as FAC 118. A&M passes in America, so Profile Records takes it, and early in 1985 it reaches the Billboard dance Top 20.

years.src: Look I've Heard · Wikipedia: Diane Charlemagne
years.h: Lindsay Reade takes over as manager; Diane Charlemagne joins
years.p: Reade, [[Tony Wilson|124a6f5d-b2e0-4a75-95ad-db4c38063e02]]'s ex-wife, starts managing the band. Beverley McDonald leaves and [[Diane Charlemagne|35508fc3-7da2-4adb-986f-2c6b79117d21]], 20, becomes the singer.

eras.title: Philadelphia and the R&B Top 10
eras.text: Out of Factory and onto Virgin's 10 Records, the band went to Philadelphia to make an R&B album and came back with a US Top 10 R&B hit. The second album, made with a jazz drummer producing, didn't chart in Britain.

years.h: 52nd Street leave Factory; bassist Derrick Johnson stays
years.p: The band follow Reade out of the label. Johnson refuses to go and remains with Factory.
years.xp: The blog history Look I've Heard describes a band split between loyalty to Factory and the pull of the majors, with Reade in the middle. Johnson's exit ends the founding rhythm section.

years.src: Wikipedia: 52nd Street (band) · Discogs: Children of the Night
years.h: Children of the Night, made in Philadelphia with Nick Martinelli
years.p: Out on 10 Records in the UK and MCA in the US. It reaches No. 71 in Britain and No. 23 on the US R&B albums chart.

years.src: Wikipedia: 52nd Street (band) · Rare and Obscure Music
yt: Tell Me (How It Feels), extended version
years.h: "Tell Me (How It Feels)" climbs to No. 8 on the US R&B chart
years.p: Fourteen weeks on Billboard's black singles chart, No. 54 in the UK. Wikipedia calls it their biggest and best-known hit.

years.h: Two more UK chart singles off Children of the Night
years.p: "You're My Last Chance" reaches No. 49 and "I Can't Let You Go" No. 57.

years.src: Discogs: 52nd Street · Rare and Obscure Music
years.p: The jazz-fusion drummer takes the chair and Michael Brecker plays saxophone. The album misses the UK chart; "I'll Return" reaches No. 79 on the US R&B chart.

years.h: John Dennison co-writes a house single for Zuzan
years.p: "Girls Can Jak Too", produced by [[Mike Pickering|5da7585b-4ac0-420f-8c58-9bb8522b459c]], comes out under the name Zuzan.

years.h: "Say You Will" is the last single, at No. 98
years.p: The last 52nd Street chart entry in Britain. Discogs says Henry kept the name afterward while the others went on as Cool Down Zone.

eras.title: Cool Down Zone and Inner City Life
eras.text: Charlemagne carried on with a new band under a new name, and in the 1990s her voice turned up on Goldie's Timeless and two UK Top 10 hits.

years.h: Charlemagne and Tony Bowry relaunch as Cool Down Zone
years.p: With live drummer Myke Wilson, they make the album New Direction; Charlemagne has writing credits on all ten songs. "Heaven Knows" reaches No. 52 in the UK.

years.src: Wikipedia: 52nd Street (band) · Rare and Obscure Music
years.h: Tony Henry starts FR'Mystery with Lorna Bailey
years.p: The duo release records on Gwarn Records from 1991 to 1994.

She becomes the main voice on [[Goldie|c5393047-0c44-48eb-b5a8-070759f04371]]'s Timeless, fronts [[Urban Cookie Collective|cb862bb0-676b-47bd-8def-b9f8b8330117]], who had two UK Top 10 hits, and sings live for [[Moby|8970d868-0723-483b-a75b-51088913d3d4]].
Charlemagne died of kidney cancer, diagnosed the year before, Wikipedia reports.

sources.title: Look I've Heard, I've Heard It All Before: Who was 52nd Street?
